sudan.title: مقتل 73 شخصا على الأقل نتيجة هجوم على سوق بمنطقة متنازع عليها بين السودان وجنوب السودان - azərtac
sudan.summary: مقتل 73 شخصا على الأقل في هجوم استهدف سوقا في منطقة متنازع عليها بين السودان وجنوب السودان. وقع الهجوم في منطقة أبيي، التي تشهد توترات مستمرة بين الجانبين. وقد أسفر الهجوم عن إصابة العديد من الأشخاص، مما يزيد من القلق بشأن الوضع الأمني في المنطقة. السلطات المحلية أكدت أن الهجوم نفذته جماعات مسلحة، مما يعكس تصاعد العنف في المناطق الحدودية. يُذكر أن منطقة أبيي تعتبر نقطة نزاع تاريخية بين السودان وجنوب السودان، حيث يسعى كلا الجانبين للسيطرة عليها.

sudan.title: الإعلان عن إضراب للمعلمين في السودان - سودان اندبندنت
sudan.summary: أعلن المعلمون في السودان عن إضراب شامل احتجاجًا على الأوضاع المعيشية الصعبة والرواتب المتدنية. يأتي هذا الإضراب في وقت تعاني فيه البلاد من أزمات اقتصادية خانقة، مما أثر سلبًا على القطاع التعليمي. وقد دعت النقابات المعنية جميع المعلمين إلى المشاركة في الإضراب الذي يهدف إلى المطالبة بتحسين الأجور وظروف العمل. وأكدت النقابات أن الإضراب سيستمر حتى تحقيق المطالب المشروعة للمعلمين، مشيرة إلى أن التعليم في السودان يحتاج إلى دعم عاجل لضمان استمرارية العملية التعليمية.

sudan.title: هجوم دامٍ لجيش السودان على سوق بأبيي.. 73 قتيلا وجوبا تستدعي سفير البرهان - العين الإخبارية
sudan.summary: شنّ جيش السودان هجوماً دامياً على سوق في منطقة أبيي، مما أسفر عن مقتل 73 شخصاً. الهجوم يأتي في وقت حساس، حيث استدعت حكومة جوبا سفير السودان، عبد الله البرهان، للتعبير عن قلقها إزاء التصعيد العسكري. وقد أدان المسؤولون في جنوب السودان الهجوم، مشيرين إلى ضرورة حماية المدنيين في المنطقة. يأتي هذا التصعيد في ظل التوترات المستمرة بين السودان وجنوب السودان، مما يزيد من المخاوف بشأن استقرار المنطقة.

sudan.title: حنين إلى «الرجل القوي».. قصة (8) ملايين مشاهدة لخبر وفاة نميري - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: تجاوزت مشاهدات خبر وفاة الرئيس السوداني الأسبق جعفر نميري ثمانية ملايين مشاهدة، مما يعكس حنين الكثيرين إلى فترة حكمه. نميري، الذي تولى السلطة في عام 1969 حتى الإطاحة به في 1985، كان شخصية مثيرة للجدل في تاريخ السودان. بعض السودانيين يتذكرونه كـ "رجل قوي" ساهم في استقرار البلاد، بينما يعتبره آخرون رمزًا للقمع. الخبر أثار تفاعلات واسعة على وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي، حيث تبادل المستخدمون ذكريات وتجارب من فترة حكمه. يعكس هذا الاهتمام العميق بتاريخه تأثيره المستمر على الوعي الجمعي للسودانيين، رغم مرور عقود على سقوط نظامه.

sudan.title: أسفر هجوم بطائرة مسيرة في السودان عن مقتل 80 شخصاً. - Vietnam.vn
sudan.summary: أسفر هجوم بطائرة مسيرة في السودان عن مقتل 80 شخصاً، حيث استهدفت الغارة منطقة في ولاية دارفور. الهجوم يأتي في وقت يشهد فيه السودان تصاعداً في النزاع المسلح بين القوات الحكومية والمجموعات المسلحة. وقد أدان المجتمع الدولي هذا الهجوم، مطالباً بتحقيق شامل لتحديد المسؤولين عنه. كما أعربت منظمات حقوق الإنسان عن قلقها إزاء تصاعد العنف وتأثيره على المدنيين. الهجوم يعكس الوضع الأمني المتدهور في البلاد، حيث يعاني السكان من تداعيات النزاع المستمر.

sudan.title: مستجدات الشرق الأوسط: أكثر من 100 قتيل في هجمات بالمسيرات في أنحاء السودان - SBS
sudan.summary: أفادت التقارير أن أكثر من 100 شخص لقوا حتفهم في سلسلة من الهجمات التي نفذتها طائرات مسيرة في مختلف أنحاء السودان. تأتي هذه الهجمات في وقت يشهد فيه البلد تصاعدًا في النزاع المسلح، حيث تتزايد الاشتباكات بين القوات الحكومية والمجموعات المسلحة. وقد أدت هذه الأحداث إلى تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية في البلاد، مع تزايد أعداد النازحين والجرحى. كما دعت منظمات حقوق الإنسان إلى ضرورة اتخاذ إجراءات عاجلة لحماية المدنيين وتقديم المساعدات اللازمة للمتضررين من هذه الهجمات.

sudan.title: السودان: أكثر من 100 قتيل في هجمات بمسيّرات على كردفان ودارفور والخرطوم - France 24
sudan.summary: أفادت تقارير أن أكثر من 100 شخص لقوا حتفهم في هجمات شنتها طائرات مسيّرة في مناطق كردفان ودارفور والخرطوم بالسودان. الهجمات، التي تُعتبر من بين الأكثر دموية في الصراع المستمر في البلاد، استهدفت مدنيين وأدت إلى تدمير العديد من المنازل والبنية التحتية. وقد أثارت هذه الأحداث قلقاً دولياً متزايداً بشأن الوضع الإنساني في السودان، حيث يعاني السكان من نقص حاد في المساعدات الأساسية. الحكومة السودانية لم تصدر بعد بياناً رسمياً حول هذه الهجمات، لكن المنظمات الإنسانية تدعو إلى اتخاذ إجراءات عاجلة لحماية المدنيين وتقديم المساعدة للمحتاجين.

sudan.title: وزير الصحة يشارك في مؤتمر وجائزة ميدغلوبال بشيكاغو - سودان اندبندنت
sudan.summary: شارك وزير الصحة في مؤتمر وجائزة ميدغلوبال الذي أقيم في شيكاغو، حيث تم مناقشة قضايا الصحة العالمية والتحديات التي تواجهها الدول. المؤتمر جمع خبراء وصناع قرار من مختلف أنحاء العالم لتبادل الأفكار والخبرات في مجال الرعاية الصحية. كما تم تسليط الضوء على الابتكارات والحلول الممكنة لتحسين الخدمات الصحية. الوزير أعرب عن أهمية التعاون الدولي في مواجهة الأوبئة والأمراض المزمنة، وأكد على التزام السودان بتحسين النظام الصحي وتوفير الرعاية اللازمة للمواطنين.

sudan.title: مجلس الأمن والدفاع يوجه بالتصدي للمخططات المهددة للبلاد - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: عقد مجلس الأمن والدفاع في السودان اجتماعًا لمناقشة التهديدات التي تواجه البلاد، حيث تم توجيه الجهات المعنية بالتصدي للمخططات التي تهدد الأمن القومي. وركز الاجتماع على التحديات الأمنية والسياسية التي يواجهها السودان، بما في ذلك الأزمات الداخلية والنزاعات. كما تم التأكيد على أهمية تعزيز التعاون بين القوات المسلحة والأجهزة الأمنية لضمان استقرار البلاد. وأشار المجلس إلى ضرورة اتخاذ إجراءات فورية لمواجهة هذه التهديدات وحماية المواطنين.

sudan.title: جوبا تستدعي السفير السوداني احتجاجًا على قصف سوق «النعام» - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: استدعت حكومة جوبا السفير السوداني احتجاجًا على القصف الذي استهدف سوق «النعام» في منطقة أبيي. وأعربت وزارة الخارجية في جنوب السودان عن إدانتها الشديدة لهذا الهجوم، الذي أسفر عن وقوع إصابات وأضرار مادية. وأكدت الحكومة أنها ستتخذ إجراءات دبلوماسية مناسبة للتعامل مع هذا الاعتداء، مشددة على أهمية الحفاظ على الأمن والاستقرار في المنطقة. يأتي هذا التصعيد في ظل التوترات المستمرة بين السودان وجنوب السودان، حيث تسعى جوبا إلى تعزيز العلاقات مع جيرانها وتفادي أي تصعيد عسكري.

ethiopia.title: Somalia's Aid Paradox - Saving Lives, Sustaining Dependency
ethiopia.content: Somalia's Aid Paradox - Saving Lives, Sustaining Dependency - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia's Aid Paradox - Saving Lives, Sustaining Dependency 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — For more than three decades, international aid has been an indispensable lifeline for Somalia. It has helped prevent humanitarian collapse, funded essential health and education services, and sustained civil-society organizations through cycles of conflict, drought, and displacement. Those contributions are real and should never be minimized. Yet prolonged reliance on external assistance raises a challenging political-economy question: can a humanitarian and development apparatus designed for immediate rescue inadvertently entrench the political arrangements and structural fragilities that perpetuate dependency? This is not an argument that external assistance has failed uniformly, that donors harbor designs to sustain instability, or that Somali institutions are passive actors. Nor does it suggest that all aid is diverted or that humanitarian organizations ignore accountability. Such sweeping claims would exceed the available evidence. The more useful inquiry concerns incentives: who sets funding priorities, who controls resources and acquires lasting capacity, who benefits commercially and politically, how much say citizens have over resources meant for them, and what happens when funding priorities change faster than public institutions can adapt. These questions are now time-sensitive because international funding is shrinking while domestic needs remain acute. The International Monetary Fund's 2025 review of Somalia estimated, from available donor information, that foreign aid may have amounted to roughly 20-30% of GDP over the preceding decade. It cautioned that comprehensive official records of total aid flows were unavailable and that most assistance was delivered outside the government budget. It also modeled possible 2025 reductions of $400-600 million, about 3-4.6% of GDP. Those were scenarios based on anticipated cuts and disbursement delays, not a measurement of every dollar ultimately lost. The World Bank's Toward Building Somalia's Social Contract adds the fiscal picture. For 2022, the federal government collected about $262 million in domestic revenue, 2.2% of GDP, while external grants financed 62% of federal spending, and 82% of official development assistance was off-budget. These are 2022 figures, not a description of Somalia's fiscal position today, but they show how thin the domestic revenue base was relative to public responsibilities. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The Overseas Development Institute's April 2026 study, Somali Systems: From Aid-Centred to State-Led Crisis Response , brings the concern into current policy. The authors of the study, Surer Mohamed and Dustin Barter, argue that the outsized role of aid and the incentives around its delivery can impede a move to state-led crisis response. They acknowledge the risks of weak transparency, accountability, and inclusion in state-led arrangements but conclude that keeping the aid-centred status quo carries greater long-term risk. As Somalia confronts shrinking funding alongside acute need, dissecting the anatomy of its aid economy is no longer only an academic exercise; it is a practical policy priority. The question is not aid versus no aid. It is whether assistance can save lives today while building the accountable institutions, domestic revenue, and public capabilities that make tomorrow's recovery less dependent on external decisions. Anatomy of aid economy Foreign assistance is rarely neutral. It is a system of decisions about authority, policy direction, and resource distribution. When external actors set funding priorities, approve project designs and manage disbursement channels, they exercise considerable influence over domestic public administration. That influence is not automatically improper. Donors answer to taxpayers and legislatures, international organizations must meet fiduciary and safeguarding standards, and humanitarian agencies need flexibility to reach people in territories where state authority is limited. Aid should not be judged solely by what it delivers today, but by the institutions and capabilities it leaves behind." In Somalia, however, the cumulative result is a crowded institutional landscape of fragmented project delivery. A donor may channel funds through an international agency, which contracts a national NGO, which then negotiates local access through customary or community intermediaries. Meanwhile, the line ministry retains only partial visibility into actual expenditure, geographic coverage, or long-term operating costs. Each link in the chain can fulfill its contractual obligations while the system as a whole remains difficult for citizens to understand or hold to account. Across health, education, water, nutrition, livelihoods, and local governance, three recurring features characterize the aid economy. The first is fragmented standards, wherein parallel project frameworks operate on different procurement rules, reporting formats, and salary scales, and because staff are trained for a project but are rarely absorbed into a lasting institutional structure, administrative capacity does not accumulate where it is most needed. The second is data isolation, where monitoring information is often routed into donor reports rather than integrated into national information systems, preventing governments from easily planning, coordinating, or evaluating. The third is vulnerable continuity, which means that services expand while a grant is active and become fragile when it closes, leaving ministries with commitments they did not choose and cannot finance. This pattern is consistent with the wider scholarship. Ken Menkhaus's work on aid and institution-building highlights the difficulty of building durable institutions through fragmented, project-based interventions, while Tobias Hagmann's Stabilization, Extraversion and Political Settlements in Somalia examines how external intervention interacts with domestic political authority. Aid also operates inside a delicate political settlement that involves the federal government, federal member states, local administrations, customary authorities, clan networks, and commercial interests. Money entering that environment interacts with existing power relationships. Its effects depend not only on the objectives written in project documents but also on who controls access, receives contracts, influences beneficiary selection, gains employment, and acquires political visibility. Aid should therefore be judged by two separate questions. First, what goods, services, and humanitarian outcomes does it deliver? Second, what political, commercial, and institutional relationships does the way it is delivered create or reinforce? A program can meet its targets and still leave little institutional legacy. An emergency response can rightly put speed above institution-building. The task is to distinguish legitimate emergency arrangements from avoidable, permanent dependency. The Bypassing Dilemma: State-building without the state Donors face a recurring choice: channel funds through public institutions burdened by capacity gaps and security risks, or deliver through international agencies with insulated risk-management systems. In acute crises, bypassing the state is often defensible. Public money should not be exposed to unacceptable risk merely to demonstrate national ownership, and life-saving relief cannot always wait for better audit or procurement systems. The damage arises when a temporary workaround hardens into permanent architecture. Repeated bypassing deprives ministries of the experience they need in procurement, program management, monitoring, and service delivery. They lack reliable expenditure data, struggle to coordinate interventions funded elsewhere, and cannot estimate the recurrent costs that follow a project's end. A self-reinforcing cycle results in three main stages. The first stage is perceived weakness, where limited administrative reach encourages donors to bypass state mechanisms. The second stage is deprived experience, in which bypassing denies ministries the opportunities to manage resources and deliver services. The third stage is perpetual fragility, where this persistent weakness is subsequently cited to justify continued circumvention. Breaking the cycle requires reciprocal commitments. Somali institutions must demonstrate fiscal integrity, keep reliable financial records, enforce procurement standards, and accept independent oversight; where they do not, external caution is legitimate. International partners, for their part, cannot expect national institutions to mature while indefinitely reserving the most consequential management functions for themselves. They should build capacity and expenditure transparency into off-budget programs from the start. The World Bank's Somalia Financial Governance Report 2025 , disclosed on 30 September 2026, examines revenue administration, public procurement, financial-sector oversight, petroleum governance, and emerging fiscal pressures, including security-sector costs. These are precisely the functions that determine whether Somalia can responsibly manage more of its own public resources over time. The strategic question is not whether all assistance should flow through government tomorrow. It is whether each off-budget program has a clear justification, a defined link to national priorities, adequate expenditure visibility, and a realistic plan to strengthen Somali capacity where appropriate. A health donor, for instance, could disclose implementing institutions, districts covered, spending categories, duration, and expected recurrent costs, while the ministry helps set service standards and reviews performance even if the donor retains financial control. A civil-service reform program should be judged not by workshops delivered but by whether recruitment becomes more competitive, payroll and personnel records improve, and essential functions continue after the project closes. Ownership vs Control: Moving beyond declarations International frameworks routinely champion national ownership; Somalia's New Deal Compact was one expression of that ambition. Yet the term can mean very different things: a government endorsing a strategy, ministries joining program design, Somali institutions controlling expenditure, or citizens and legislators shaping and scrutinizing priorities. These are not equivalent, and the first is far easier to achieve than the last. A government can endorse a national development plan while lacking influence over the resources needed to implement it. A ministry can attend coordination meetings without controlling a single funding decision. A national strategy can become the reference document for dozens of projects while nobody holds reliable information on their combined spending or future operating costs. Ownership then remains a political declaration rather than an operational capability. The gap widens when donors operate across different geographic zones, apply separate funding cycles and reporting rules, and work around federal ministries. Each project may be individually defensible, yet the collective pattern is uneven: one district receives overlapping interventions while another is underserved, and a ministry with a national mandate lacks the staff to coordinate externally financed work. Federalism adds a further layer, because member states may receive assistance through several international channels, complicating coordination between national and subnational levels. None of this requires bad faith. Organizations rationally pursue their own mandates, yet the combined outcome is less effective than a coordinated one. A more substantive definition of ownership is needed, anchored in demonstrable influence over planning, transparent expenditure tracking, and public accountability. At the same time, ownership cannot be a euphemism for unaccountable political control over donor resources. A credible national system requires transparent procurement, legislative scrutiny, independent oversight, and genuine avenues for citizens to participate and to challenge decisions. The aim is not to swap donor control for unaccountable domestic control but to allocate responsibilities clearly and hold both domestic and international actors to their commitments. Fiscal Foundations: Reconnecting revenue to social contract Taxation is more than a way of raising money; it is part of the fiscal cement that binds citizens to the state. Taxpayers have a stronger claim to explanations about spending and service quality, and governments that depend on domestic revenue have stronger reasons to engage constructively with taxpayers and the businesses that sustain the economy. Taxation does not automatically produce democracy, and domestic revenue can itself be captured by political or commercial interests. Even so, the link between revenue and accountability matters for Somalia's state-building debate. The question is not aid versus no aid, but whether assistance can save lives today while building institutions that make tomorrow's recovery less dependent on external decisions." The 2022 World Bank figures cited above illustrate the historical imbalance: federal domestic revenue of about 2.2% of GDP, combined federal and member-state revenue of about 3.6%, and external grants financing 62% of federal expenditure. When public services are financed by actors who are not answerable to domestic political processes, the feedback loop between taxation, representation, and accountability remains underdeveloped. Citizens may not know which institution is responsible for a service, and government may be blamed for failures it has no means to prevent. The problem is not simply that Somalia collects too little tax. It is whether the collection is equitable, predictable, transparent, and tied to visible improvements in services. Where households and businesses face multiple charges, informal payments, or unpredictable levies while public services remain weak, taxation deepens distrust rather than building the social contract. Somalia, therefore, needs a dual reform: expanding lawful domestic revenue while making its use more transparent and responsive to public needs. Somaliland offers a useful but qualified comparison. In Taxation, Political Accountability and Foreign Aid: Lessons from Somaliland , Nicholas Eubank argued that Somaliland's limited access to foreign assistance increased the importance of local tax revenue and gave actors outside government leverage to demand more inclusive and accountable institutions. Sarah Phillips's When Less Was More likewise stresses the role of local ownership in the formative settlement, while noting the exclusionary limits of elite bargaining. Later scholarship, such as Somaliland's Authoritarian Turn , documents the risks of oligarchic influence and concentrated economic power. The lesson is not that less aid automatically produces better governance. Somaliland's path reflected a distinctive history of conflict, customary negotiation, and local institution-building, and limited aid was one factor among several. A sudden reduction in Somalia could devastate essential services without producing more representative institutions. The comparison is best treated as a hypothesis about revenue bargaining, namely that stronger domestic mobilization, combined with transparent spending and meaningful participation, can create a more durable basis for accountability. Managing Vulnerability: Gatekeeping, diversion risks Humanitarian operations function in environments where access often depends on negotiation with regional authorities, landowners, customary leaders, and commercial intermediaries. These relationships can be vital for safe passage, staff protection, and community acceptance, and local knowledge is often indispensable. But they also create risks of exclusion, manipulation, and diversion. The question is how systems of access and influence affect who actually receives what has been allocated. The independent Inter-Agency Humanitarian Evaluation of the Response to the Humanitarian Crisis in Somalia , published in 2025 (see also the UNFPA overview ), assessed the collective famine-prevention response of 2021-2024. It found that the scaled-up response played a critical role in preventing famine and saving lives. It also identified weaknesses in accountability, inclusion, coordination, and the management of diversion risk, noting that the rapid expansion of assistance in 2022 initially gave insufficient attention to the growing risk of diversion. Later reforms improved cooperation and transparency but took longer than envisaged. The evaluation further noted that the full 2023 post-distribution diversion investigation remained confidential, with access limited to selected stakeholders. Confidentiality can be justified to protect investigations, personal safety, or due process, but it is a transparency issue worth recognizing. These findings must be read carefully, as they show that diversion risks were serious enough to warrant investigation and system-wide reform, but they do not show that every program was compromised or that diversion occurred at the same scale everywhere. Three structural vulnerabilities stand out. The first is initial blind spots, where rapid scale-ups during acute crises can underestimate and under-manage escalating diversion risk. The second is registration challenges, in which digital beneficiary registries can improve auditing and prevent duplication, but if selection itself reflects unequal access to local power, technology can make an exclusionary allocation more efficient because better data cannot show whether the criteria are fair. The third is oversight gaps, meaning that third-party monitoring must go beyond confirming that goods reached a location and should instead verify that recipients received their full entitlements, that no unauthorized deductions occurred, that people were not excluded because of identity or status, and that complaints can be made safely. The World Food Programme's 2024 targeting pilots in Baidoa and Dolow, discussed in a December 2025 ODI report , explored ways to improve targeting and protect the integrity of unconditional cash and voucher assistance. Their lesson is that integrity depends on attention to power, not merely on better forms, software, and audit procedures. Commercial rents, political competition A large injection of foreign aid also creates demand for logistics, transport, security, construction, communications, consultancy, and financial services. These markets create jobs and stimulate local economic activity. They can also concentrate benefits among narrow networks with privileged access to information and decision-makers. Somalia's wider political economy sharpens the point. Movement corridors, ports, checkpoints, and aid procurement can generate substantial income entangled with political and security arrangements. PeaceRep's September 2026 analysis, "A Decade on, Somalia's Federal Pact Benefits Elites and Al-Shabaab ," draws on several hundred interviews across Somalia and the diaspora. It identifies two connected themes: control of movement through checkpoints and control, mismanagement, or manipulation of international aid. Its authors argue that political elites and business allies can profit from aid-related rents and economic chokepoints. These are the researchers' interpretations of their evidence, not proof that every official, business, or aid organization is implicated. Further material is available on PeaceRep's Somalia page . ethiopia.title: #Daily_Brief: Netanyahu map depicts #Ethiopia, #Sudan’s RSF as ‘friendly’ to #Israel, #UAE - Addis Standard
ethiopia.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has released a map indicating that Ethiopia and Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are considered "friendly" to Israel and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). This development highlights a shift in regional alliances and reflects Israel's growing diplomatic engagement with African nations. The map aims to strengthen ties with these countries amid ongoing geopolitical changes in the region. Netanyahu's government is actively seeking to expand Israel's influence in Africa, which has been a focus of Israeli foreign policy in recent years. The implications of this map could affect Israel's relationships with neighboring countries and its strategic interests in Africa.

ethiopia.title: From Military Victory to Political Settlement - Why Ethiopia's Real Test Lies Beyond Controlling Mekelle
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: From Military Victory to Political Settlement - Why Ethiopia's Real Test Lies Beyond Controlling Mekelle - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: From Military Victory to Political Settlement - Why Ethiopia's Real Test Lies Beyond Controlling Mekelle 19 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Mekelle, the capital of Tigray Regional State, has now changed hands three times in six years. Federal forces took the city in November 2020, within a month of the last war beginning; Tigrayan forces retook it in June 2021 . On 3 October 2026, federal troops and the allied Tigray Peace Force entered it again , after the TPLF announced that it had withdrawn and that its regional administration would "temporarily move out" of the capital. The mood in parts of Addis Abeba is triumphant. It should be sober. This round began on 23 September, when Tigrayan forces launched an offensive into Afar and Amhara . The momentum soon reversed; government-aligned forces have since also entered Adigrat , near the Eritrean border, and Axum . On 11 October, according to local media, Getachew Reda, now the prime minister's adviser on East African affairs, declared the war over and said Tigray would be run by a federal command post for six months before elections. The TPLF leadership, now in the northern countryside, has announced a shift to "mobile warfare." Taking a city is a military event. Settling the question that produced the war is sociological: who belongs to the political community, on what terms, and who has the authority to decide. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines My argument is this. The war is rooted in an unresolved bargain at home; the regional realignment that now sets rival Gulf- and Egypt-led alignments against each other across the Horn raises its stakes and supplies its patrons. Ethiopia is stronger in external terms than at any point since 2018, yet thinner in the social foundations of authority: the willing consent of its own regions. Whether Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed emerges as the Horn's pivotal statesman or as the manager of a permanent counterinsurgency depends on what Addis Abeba does with Mekelle, not on the fact of having taken it. Tigray's unfinished peace, Ethiopia's unsettled state The federal government's case deserves to be stated at full strength, because much of it is sound. The Pretoria Agreement of 2022 required the disarmament of Tigrayan forces, and disputes over disarmament and the TPLF's legal status were never resolved . In 2025 a TPLF faction forced Getachew Reda out of the interim administration ; in May 2026 the party reinstated the pre-war regional council, which elected Debretsion Gebremichael as president , outside the framework Pretoria had set. By mid-year, Tigray's authorities were declaring that the agreement "has collapsed," and on 23 September, it was Tigrayan forces that went on the offensive. No sovereign state tolerates a second army answering to a rival government. That case is strong, but it is not the whole account. A detailed Al Jazeera reconstruction found that while the TPLF retained an organizational and security role the agreement was meant to diminish , the federal government also failed to deliver important parts of the settlement. The June national elections were not held in Tigray at all . Meanwhile, Tigrayans lived what a contributor in these pages called peace on paper and suffering in practice . By May, Addis Standard was reporting allegations of forced conscription across Tigray , with opposition parties such as Salsay Weyane Tigray demanding an end to what Tigrayans call gifa. Prolonged deprivation converts political grievance into everyday humiliation, the raw material of mobilization. Tigrayan dissent also shows that Tigray is not a single political subject. Any settlement that treats the TPLF as the sole voice of Tigray, or all Tigrayans as the TPLF, will misread the society it seeks to pacify. Taking a city is a military event. Settling the question that produced the war is sociological." By September, Ethiopia contained two authorities claiming to govern the same territory, each with its own army. Charles Tilly called this condition multiple sovereignty and treated it as the defining feature of a revolutionary situation. The war is therefore less about resources or ideology than about statehood: whether Ethiopia's federation is a union of self-governing nations that may bargain with the center by force or a sovereign state that monopolizes legitimate coercion and negotiates only through its institutions. Alliance of the aggrieved Days before the offensive, seven armed movements, including the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army, announced an alliance pledging to work toward the fall of Abiy's government and its replacement by a charter-based transitional administration. Fano fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF in 2020-2022 , and Amhara and Tigrayan nationalists still claim the same land in Western Tigray. Sociologically, this is a negative coalition, bound by a shared adversary rather than a shared vision. Such coalitions are strong at the moment of mobilization and brittle at the moment of distribution, because what each member ultimately wants is indivisible: Welkait cannot belong to both Amhara and Tigray. The fissures also run through, not merely between, these constituencies. The Tigray Peace Force, a Tigrayan militia aligned with Addis Abeba , helped take Alamata and entered Mekelle beside federal troops, and Getachew Reda, once the TPLF's most visible spokesman, returned to the city as the face of federal authority. The war over Tigray is also, increasingly, a war within it. Yet a fractious coalition is not an impotent one. Fano holds towns in southern Wollo and northern Shewa , and the TPLF left Mekelle without a street battle, preserving its fighters, much as it withdrew to the highlands in 2020 before returning in 2021. Analysts at the Critical Threats Project judge the movement weaker than in the last war , citing thinner popular support and Ethiopia's improved drones. They may be right. But insurgencies need not win battles; they need only outlast a state's patience. After Mekelle: Control without consent The capture of Mekelle by federal forces has not ended multiple sovereignty; it has changed its form. Two governments in one region have become a government in the towns and an insurgency in the hills. The question now is whether the authority that holds Mekelle can become one Tigrayans obey without being compelled. The first days show how steep that climb will be. Federal forces did not inherit a city ready to be governed. Residents described a security vacuum and looting of government offices , and the UN reported that warehouses run by a UN agency and aid organizations had been looted . The fighting has been costly: hospital sources told the BBC that at least 52 civilians were killed in three days around Alamata , and a humanitarian source estimated at least 150,000 displaced in Afar . All this falls on a region already in drought, where, according to the regional disaster agency, 3.9 million people, more than half the population, needed emergency food assistance . An administration that arrives by arms will be judged by bread, and it will be judged quickly. A command post followed by elections has a logic, but it is an instrument of what sociologist Michael Mann called despotic power , the capacity to act without negotiating with society. Despotic power can take a city; only infrastructural power, the routine capacity to deliver law and services with local cooperation, can hold it. The Tigray Peace Force gives the federal presence a Tigrayan face, but it also risks turning a federal-regional war into an intra-Tigrayan one, in which those who fought beside Addis Abeba are seen by their neighbors as agents of conquest. Success over the next six months will be measured not in towns held but in whether cash, fuel, and food move; whether the displaced of Western Tigray can go home; and whether Tigrayans who belong to neither the TPLF nor the Tigray Peace Force can organize, compete, and win. Mandate and monopoly The Prosperity Party comfortably won June's elections , taking 438 of the 486 seats for which results were declared . The vote supplied a procedural mandate. It could not, by itself, supply what Max Weber treated as the substance of legitimacy: a belief among the governed that authority is rightful. Elections were not held in Tigray, Fano has held swathes of the Amhara countryside since 2023 , and the OLA has fought in Oromia since 2018. Before the vote, an Addis Standard op-ed described the ruling party's method as procedural authoritarianism , power exercised through rather than against formal institutions. Where institutions cannot carry competition, it migrates to arms. The National Dialogue Commission might have been a bridge, yet even its Tigray agenda-gathering forum had to be moved to Addis Abeba . Battlefield success can deepen state authority; Tilly's observation that war made the state is not wrong. But in Ethiopia, war has unmade regimes as often as it has made them; the Derg fell to a coalition of regional fronts. The temptation after Mekelle will be to treat armed opponents purely as criminals rather than as expressions of unresolved political questions. A Tigray election held under a command post, without credible guarantees for the TPLF's rivals or a path back for its rank and file, would reproduce the June pattern at regional scale: a mandate without consent. Abiy's two ledgers The external ledger is strong. In June, the IMF reported improving output, exports, reserves, and revenue, alongside declining inflation , as it reached agreement on the fifth review of Ethiopia's program. By external measures, Abiy is stronger than at any point in his tenure. The domestic ledger is harder. The coalition now arrayed against him includes his two most important wartime partners of 2020: Fano and Eritrea. Supporters of the government will say each broke away over its own ambitions: Fano over the reorganization of regional special forces , Asmara over a Pretoria process to which it was not a party . Critics see a pattern in which alliances rest on personal bargains rather than institutions and dissolve once those bargains are spent. Either way, Ethiopia's wartime friendships have proved less durable than its enmities. The 2019 Nobel laureate, honored for making peace with Eritrea, now accuses Asmara of sending troops into Tigray. In a February letter to Addis Standard, former foreign minister Gedu Andargachew said that Eritrean and Ethiopian forces operated "as a single force" until the Pretoria ceasefire , an account that contradicts the prime minister's own. An unreckoned war tends to seed the next one. If military advantage is now followed by political inclusion, Abiy will emerge as the Horn's indispensable statesman. If it is followed by reprisal and exclusion, he risks winning a war and losing the peace for a second time. Access to the sea and the logic of encirclement No issue has shaped the regional reading of this war more than Abiy's quest for the sea. He has called the loss of Assab a historical mistake whose reversal is "a matter of time," while insisting that Ethiopia has no intention to invade Eritrea . The war has turned that ambition into a concrete vulnerability. Fighting in Afar threatened the routes from Djibouti through which most Ethiopian imports, including fuel, pass . A state of Ethiopia's size that depends on a single corridor through a contested borderland is not simply a trading nation with a logistics problem; it is a sovereignty with a hostage. Since Mekelle fell, the Eritrean dimension has moved from allegation towards confrontation. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of a territorial incursion and demanded the withdrawal of its troops and told the UN Security Council that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 kilometers into Tigray . Asmara denies any incursion and has asked the Council to intervene , calling Ethiopia's conduct a pretext to seize Assab. The scale of any Eritrean deployment has not been independently established. But on 5 October, in his re-inauguration address, Abiy reiterated that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea . Maritime access, national security, and the war have fused into one question. Addis Abeba's practical response has been quieter than its rhetoric and probably wiser. On 24 September, Abiy stood beside Djibouti's President Ismail Omar Guelleh to announce a $660 million refined-fuel pipeline from Damerjog to Dewele . The pipeline makes a neighbor a stakeholder in Ethiopia's security rather than an object of its ambition. This magazine warned in 2024 that a country ravaged by internal crises can neither shape nor safeguard its national interest . The most serious threat to Ethiopia's maritime lifeline in 2026 has come not from foreign navies but from fighting in Afar, Amhara, and Tigray. Sea access is a legitimate national aspiration, but its first line of defense runs through domestic peace. Two blocs, both fluid Those coastal anxieties have found patrons. The Institute for Economics and Peace describes an emerging UAE-Israel-Ethiopia axis set against a Saudi-Egypt-Türkiye reaction . In July, Saudi Arabia launched a 14-nation Red Sea maritime coalition that included Egypt, Türkiye, Sudan, Djibouti, and Somalia, but not the UAE. On 4 October, the day after Mekelle fell, the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia, and Sudan converged at El Alamein; their declaration did not name Ethiopia but asserted that Red Sea governance belongs to littoral states and restated Egypt's demands on the dam . Sudan is where the blocs collide. Sudan's army-aligned government has alleged that drone attacks on its territory originated from Ethiopia , which Addis Abeba rejects as baseless , and a Reuters investigation reported that Ethiopia was hosting an RSF training camp . Ethiopia's army chief, in turn, accuses foreign powers of "pushing, supporting, and supplying" the new alliance , naming Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt, all of which deny it. On 1 October, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats ; Asmara severed relations . Whatever the truth of each allegation, proxy war is a currency that circulates in both directions. Ethiopia has won wars before. What it has rarely done is win the peace that follows." The Nile runs through the same ledger. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam was inaugurated in September 2025 , and in February Cairo denied a report that it had offered to help Ethiopia secure Red Sea access in exchange for flexibility on the dam. The two dossiers have become one bargaining space. No battle changes hydrology; what war changes is the cost of Egyptian pressure. If Ethiopia emerges cohesive, pressure exerted through its internal fault lines loses value. If the war drags on, Cairo gains leverage without firing a shot. These alignments are not alliances. Somalia joined the El Alamein summit yet kept cooperating with Addis Abeba, and its president met Abiy as recently as 28 September . Ethiopia's BRICS membership, shared with Egypt and the UAE , is insurance, not protection. Washington, which let its Eritrea sanctions lapse, citing US interests in the Red Sea while also imposing visa restrictions on "hardline members" of the TPLF , offers neutrality, not guarantees. Neither camp can impose an order on the Horn. The decisive variable is Ethiopia's internal cohesion: a united Ethiopia is a regional pole; a divided one is a regional battlefield. The first is coerced consolidation, and it is now the government's declared path: a command post, a coalition fragmenting along its fault lines, and separate settlements with its members. It can succeed only if it brings a credible process on the disputed territories, reconstruction, an election open to Tigrayans of every persuasion, and a national dialogue that includes those who fought. That requires a political generosity the government has not yet demonstrated. The second is protracted insurgency. The TPLF has given up the towns, not the war. Its leaders have promised further operations from the northern highlands, the terrain from which it returned in 2021. A mobile campaign alongside Fano and the OLA would mean a war of attrition that drains the economy and invites proxy intervention. The third is regionalization, and it is no longer hypothetical: severed diplomatic relations, rival letters to the Security Council, and reported Eritrean deployments on Ethiopian soil, layered onto Sudan's war. The EU has urged both governments to de-escalate , and the International Crisis Group has called for former AU envoy Olusegun Obasanjo to be brought back into mediation and for Saudi Arabia and the UAE to coordinate to keep a Red Sea front from opening. The fourth is a positive-sum Ethiopia. It reaches the sea not by redrawing borders but by rewriting interests: a guaranteed port and corridor arrangement in which Eritrea keeps sovereignty, Ethiopia holds equity and access, and neighbors share in its markets. The dam generated 52 percent of Ethiopia's electricity-export revenue in 2025/26 , according to the state utility; the planned Bishoftu airport is billed as Africa's largest ; and a population of some 135 million could make Ethiopia the Horn's energy, logistics, and manufacturing center. The current confrontation makes this harder, not impossible, provided Addis Abeba trades the language of restitution for that of interdependence. Without peace, a young population becomes a recruiting pool rather than a dividend. The darker variant of success is a garrison state with a port: a coastline without peace, power without legitimacy. Decisive Victory: Political, not military The strongest possibility is a civic turn. Both camps in this war are multi-ethnic coalitions, each discovering that no ethnic project can secure itself alone. Sea-access nationalism already addresses citizens as Ethiopians rather than as members of ethnic nations, but it cannot substitute for a negotiated federal bargain. Exhaustion, a generation born after 1991 and integrating national markets, could yield a different consensus: citizenship as the basis of political claims, cultural rights protected, Article 39 reinterpreted by agreement, electoral rules rewarding cross-regional parties, and disputed territories under shared administration. Imposed from above, civic nationalism becomes assimilation; it must be chosen, in Renan's phrase, as a daily plebiscite. The balance of power in the Horn will not finally be decided at Assab, at the dam, or in Mekelle. It will be decided by whether the Ethiopian state can turn the loyalty of its citizens from a battlefield into a resource. This is the paradox of Ethiopian power: the more Ethiopia acts as a regional power, the more its internal fault lines become assets for its rivals. Abiy has shown he can survive, outmaneuver, and project; the question is whether he can include. Ethiopia has won wars before. What it has rarely done is win the peace that follows. That, not the fall of any city, is the victory worth seeking. AS Editor's Note : Tesfatsion Dominiko has a PhD in Sociology and Social Anthropology from Stellenbosch University. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's recent military control of Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, marks a significant shift in the ongoing conflict, which has seen the city change hands multiple times since 2020. Federal forces, alongside the Tigray Peace Force, re-entered Mekelle on October 3, 2026, following the TPLF's withdrawal. While the mood in Addis Ababa is celebratory, the situation remains complex. The war's roots lie in unresolved political grievances, with multiple authorities claiming governance over Tigray. The federal government faces challenges in establishing legitimacy and authority, as many Tigrayans view the TPLF as their representative. The humanitarian crisis in the region is dire, with millions needing assistance. The future stability of Ethiopia hinges on whether the federal government can gain the consent of Tigrayans and address the underlying sociopolitical issues rather than merely exert military control.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Warns Somaliland Recognition Could Strengthen Al-Shabaab, Somaliland Officials Push Back
ethiopia.content: Somalia: Ethiopia Warns Somaliland Recognition Could Strengthen Al-Shabaab, Somaliland Officials Push Back - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Somalia: Ethiopia Warns Somaliland Recognition Could Strengthen Al-Shabaab, Somaliland Officials Push Back 19 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia has warned that recognizing Somaliland could undermine regional counterterrorism efforts and strengthen Al-Shabaab, while Somaliland officials have rejected the security concerns, arguing that recognition would instead enhance regional stability and advance Ethiopia's economic and strategic interests. Speaking to i24NEWS' Middle East Now , Ethiopia's ambassador to Israel, Tesfaye Yetaye Anteneh, said recognition could prompt Somalia to demand the withdrawal of Ethiopian troops deployed in the country as part of regional counterterrorism operations. "The moment, for example, Ethiopia recognizes Somaliland, the Somali government will request Ethiopia to withdraw its troops from Somalia," Anteneh said, warning that Al-Shabaab could exploit the resulting security vacuum to launch attacks in Somalia, Somaliland and potentially Ethiopia. The ambassador's remarks come amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia and escalating tensions between Addis Abeba and Asmara, raising concerns about a wider regional confrontation . Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of violating its sovereignty by deploying troops inside Ethiopian territory, allegations Eritrea has rejected while accusing the Ethiopian government of preparing an "unprovoked war of aggression." Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Anteneh said Eritrean forces remained in five localities in the Irob area of northern Ethiopia and called on the international community to pressure Asmara to withdraw its troops. Eritrea has also denied supporting Tigrayan rebel forces. Somaliland rejects security concerns Saeed Ibrahim, editor of the Somaliland Chronicle, challenged Ethiopia's assessment, arguing that Somaliland's record of preventing Al-Shabaab from establishing a significant operational presence within its territory undermines the ambassador's concerns. "I just don't agree with him," Ibrahim said during the i24NEWS programme, adding that he expected Ethiopia and Somaliland to resume negotiations over maritime access because of their closely aligned economic and strategic interests. Somaliland's ambassador to Israel, Mohamed Hagi, similarly argued in an October 15 post on X that recognizing the territory would strengthen Ethiopia's security rather than expose it to additional threats. "I am convinced the opposite is true: Ethiopia stands to gain enormous strategic, economic, and security benefits by recognising Somaliland, with zero security threat," Hagi wrote. He described Somaliland as "a strategic asset, not a security liability," citing its record against Al-Shabaab and piracy. Hagi also argued that Somalia's growing relationships with Ethiopia's regional rivals posed a greater strategic concern for Addis Abeba than Somaliland's pursuit of international recognition. Ethiopia's pursuit of sea access Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea's independence in 1993 and remains heavily dependent on neighbouring Djibouti for maritime trade. Anteneh described securing sea access as an economic and strategic necessity for a country with a population exceeding 130 million. In January 2024, Ethiopia and Somaliland signed a memorandum of understanding proposing access to the coastline and the possibility of diplomatic recognition. The agreement triggered strong opposition from Somalia, which considers Somaliland part of its sovereign territory. Ethiopia has yet to formally recognize Somaliland, despite Israel becoming the first United Nations member state to do so in December 2025. Somaliland officials maintain that recognition would provide Ethiopia with economic opportunities through the strategic Port of Berbera on the Gulf of Aden while strengthening cooperation on regional security. The dispute has gained renewed international attention following remarks by US President Donald Trump describing Somaliland as a "totally different country" from Somalia. Although the comments prompted celebrations in Somaliland's capital, Hargeisa, no formal change in US recognition policy has been announced. For Addis Abeba, the question remains how to balance its pursuit of maritime access with its security cooperation with Somalia and the diplomatic consequences of recognizing Somaliland. ethiopia.title: Oromo Intellectuals Back Ola-Fano Membership in New Armed Alliance, Call for Inclusive Transition in Ethiopia
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Oromo Intellectuals Back Ola-Fano Membership in New Armed Alliance, Call for Inclusive Transition in Ethiopia - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Oromo Intellectuals Back Ola-Fano Membership in New Armed Alliance, Call for Inclusive Transition in Ethiopia 19 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — A group of Oromo intellectuals and public figures has backed the Oromo Liberation Army's (OLA) participation in a newly formed opposition coalition that includes the Amhara Fano movement, describing the alliance as a potential opening to address Ethiopia's deepening political crisis while calling for an inclusive transition that safeguards the rights and political aspirations of all communities. In a statement released Saturday October 17, and titled "Statement by Oromo Intellectuals on Ethiopia's Political Crisis and the Need for an Inclusive Transition," the signatories described the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Coalition for Survival, also known as the Alliance for Survival, and the OLA's participation in it as "a significant first step toward finding a way out of a protracted crisis." The statement comes amid a widening debate among Oromo political constituencies over the OLA's decision to join forces with movements whose historical grievances, political objectives and national aspirations differ significantly from those of the Oromo. While some question whether the alignment can "safeguard Oromo interests", others frame the coalition as a "northern front" against a government led by an Oromo prime minister. Supporters, meanwhile, argue that Ethiopia's interlocking conflicts and political grievances require cooperation among opposition forces that have long operated separately. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The intellectuals' statement makes the case for the third position, arguing that historical antagonisms should not prevent political cooperation when the country faces a crisis that threatens its stability and the rights of its peoples. However, their endorsement is accompanied by a warning that removing the current government would not, by itself, guarantee democracy, peace or justice. "The weakening or removal of an existing political order does not automatically produce democracy, peace, or justice," the signatories said, urging the alliance and other political stakeholders to establish a credible, inclusive transitional process. A new alliance amid Ethiopia's fractured opposition landscape The Alliance for Survival was announced on September 20, 2026 , bringing together seven opposition and armed groups: the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), the OLA, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar National United Revolutionary Front (ANURF), the Benishangul Peoples' Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples' Democratic Movement. The coalition announced its intention to "remove" Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government militarily and establish a transitional administration, citing nationwide insecurity, armed conflict, displacement, poverty and human rights violations. For far too long, Ethiopia's opposition political landscape has been characterized by cycles of violence, mutual suspicion, and division Its formation brought together groups with distinct political objectives and constituencies, including former adversaries associated with the war in the Tigray region. Internationally, the alliance's formation drew criticism from several countries and blocs, including the European Union . Less widely reported, however, is the debate it has sparked among Oromos in Ethiopia and abroad, which made OLA's participation particularly contentious because of the historical and political divisions between Oromo and Amhara constituencies and the competing interpretations of what cooperation with Fano could mean for Oromo national aspirations. The intellectuals argue that Ethiopia's opposition landscape has been weakened by fragmentation, mutual suspicion and conflicts between communities that have diverted attention from underlying political grievances. "For far too long, Ethiopia's opposition political landscape has been characterized by cycles of violence, mutual suspicion, and division," they said. They further accused the government of repeatedly turning legitimate political grievances into "horizontal conflicts between communities," deepening mistrust and ethnic antagonisms while making collective political solutions more difficult. The statement's central argument is that Ethiopia's multiple conflicts cannot be resolved sustainably if political forces remain divided along historical, ethnic and ideological lines. OLA-Fano alignment divides Oromo opinion The OLA's participation has intensified debate among Oromo political constituencies, with disagreements centering on whether cooperation with Fano is a necessary strategic response to the national crisis or a potentially damaging compromise of Oromo political interests. One position rejects the alliance on the grounds that a shared opposition to the federal government does not resolve fundamental differences over national self-determination, historical accountability, territory and security. Supporters of this perspective argue that the OLA cooperation with Fano will not "subordinate Oromo aspirations" to a broader coalition's political objectives. A second position interprets the alliance as a "northern political and military front" against a government led by an Oromo prime minister. Supporters of this framing present the OLA's participation as contradictory to the movement's stated commitment to "Oromo rights and political aspirations." A third position defends the coalition as a pragmatic response to a nationwide crisis that individual opposition movements have been unable to resolve independently. Its proponents argue that cooperation need not mean "ideological convergence or the abandonment of distinct national aspirations"; rather, it can create an opportunity to pursue a common political opening while addressing disagreements through negotiation. The intellectuals' statement aligns with the third position, arguing that Oromo political aspirations and rights must remain central to any political process without being pursued in isolation from the legitimate aspirations of other peoples. "Whatever differences exist regarding the country's past and future, the peoples of Ethiopia must not be made enemies of one another while their common political grievances remain unresolved and their shared future uncertain," they said. "The struggle for justice and freedom must not become a struggle between communities," the statement added. The argument places responsibility on the alliance to demonstrate that its members can cooperate without sacrificing the rights, dignity and political agency of the communities they claim to represent. OLA leadership defends participation The debate has also drawn responses from the OLA leadership . OLA leader Kumsa Dirribaa, popularly known as Jaal Marroo, and his senior adviser, Jaal Jireenyaa Guddataa , have appeared in various media interviews to defend the decision of the group to participate in the coalition. Jaal Marroo admitted that there were around 20 meetings that took place between OLA and the remaining members of the Alliance prior to its announcement. Both have also argued that the OLA should not remain isolated from other opposition forces at a time when the Oromo people are facing what they describe as one of "the most brutal regimes" in their history. In the letter issued over the weekend, the group of intellectuals and public figures do not dismiss the concerns being raised in the ongoing debates. They call on Oromo civic actors, intellectuals and political stakeholders to scrutinize the alliance's objectives, commitments and long-term implications, while cautioning against rejecting it reflexively because of historical antagonisms or partisan interests. "Legitimate questions concerning emerging political alignments, their objectives, commitments, and long-term implications must be examined openly and critically," they said. The crisis now engulfing the entire country began in Oromia eight years ago The statement also urges the alliance and its constituent organizations to establish "credible mechanisms for resolving disagreements." Intellectuals link national crisis to grievances in Oromia The signatories argue that the crisis now affecting Ethiopia has deep roots in Oromia, where the conflict between government forces and the OLA has persisted for years. "The crisis now engulfing the entire country began in Oromia eight years ago," the statement said. The intellectuals also cited a statement they attributed to the head of the Oromia Prosperity Party: "We do not bother to catch the fish (the OLA); we will rather drain the sea (the Oromo)." They argue that the statement reflected a policy of collective punishment against the Oromo population, which they describe as the OLA's social base, and contend that the consequences included civilian deaths, displacement and widespread suffering. These are allegations and characterizations made by the signatories. Their broader argument is that militarized responses to political opposition have contributed to a nationwide crisis in which multiple communities face insecurity, displacement and political exclusion. "A political arrangement that protects the rights, dignity, and agency of all communities offers a more sustainable basis for addressing the country's interconnected crises," they said. Cooperation does not require forgetting history. It requires confronting history honestly and refusing to remain its prisoners For the signatories, the challenge is to ensure that cooperation across political divides does not come at the expense of Oromo aspirations or the rights of other communities. Call for a credible and inclusive transition The intellectuals' most consequential qualification concerns what would follow the removal of the current government. They warn that without a credible transitional arrangement, Ethiopia risks reproducing existing patterns of exclusion and political domination under a different configuration of power. The statement calls for a process involving "all relevant political stakeholders, including armed and unarmed opposition groups, civil society, and representatives of Ethiopia's diverse nations and nationalities." Such a transition, the signatories argue, must respect distinct political identities and legitimate national aspirations, protect civilians and allow Ethiopia's peoples to determine their political future freely, without coercion or predetermined outcomes. The signatories called on the Alliance to move beyond military coordination and develop a credible political framework capable of accommodating its members' divergent objectives. The statement, signed by prominent figures including Professor Mohammed Hassan, Professor Ezekiel Gabbisa, Baqqalaa Garbaa, Dr. Milkeessaa Miidhagaa, Dr. Bayaan Asoobaa and Jaal Jireenyaa Guddataa, presents cooperation as an opportunity to break from the fragmentation that has characterized Ethiopia's opposition politics . "Cooperation does not require forgetting history," the signatories said. "It requires confronting history honestly and refusing to remain its prisoners." Read the original article on Addis Standard .
